sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: WFP Cuts Gaza Food Aid by Third Due to Funding Shortages
cards.content: The World Food Programme (WFP) is forced to drastically reduce its food aid to the Gaza Strip due to funding shortages. This means that the number of people helped by the WFP will drop by about a third, from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves. The reduced aid will affect the daily hot meals provided by community kitchens, which will decrease from 250,000 to 150,000, and families living in hard-to-reach areas will receive a meal every other day instead of daily. The WFP's Palestine director, Shaun Hughes, emphasized that the cuts are due to finances, not a decrease in need. The agency urgently needs $450m to maintain critical operations over the next six months.

cards.title: Austrian Airlines Flight Makes Emergency Landing in Bulgaria
cards.content: Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to make an emergency landing in Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat. The Airbus A320 plane, carrying 51 passengers and six crew members, took off from Tel Aviv and was heading to Vienna when it was diverted to Sofia. The flight was escorted by a Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jet, and authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed. The incident comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv last month. The investigation into the threat has begun, and no injuries have been reported.

cards.title: Man dies in Dublin assault; Gardaí appeal for witnesses
cards.content: A man in his late 30s, named Jamie Bailey, died after a fatal assault in Dublin. He was found with serious injuries on a footpath in Blackhorse Place early Sunday morning and pronounced dead at the hospital. The area has been cordoned off for a forensic examination, and a post-mortem will determine the cause of death. Gardaí are appealing to anyone who was in the area between 2am and 3:30am to come forward. The investigation is being led from an incident room at the Bridewell Garda Station.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: ChangXin Predicts Profitability in 2026, Driven by AI Demand Growth
cards.content: a Chinese chipmaker, ChangXin Memory Technologies, expects to reverse a net loss and become profitable in the first nine months of 2026, with a predicted net profit of 131-132.5 billion yuan. The company's revenue is also expected to increase by 232.9-237.9 billion yuan, driven by growing demand for AI computing power. This growth has led to supply shortages and higher prices in the global DRAM market. ChangXin has been gaining ground in the global memory chip market, now accounting for 10% of global DRAM revenue, up from 5% a year earlier.

cards.title: White dwarfs have unexpected colors, including green, pink, and purple, study finds.
cards.content: In a groundbreaking study, astronomers from the University of Warwick have discovered that white dwarfs, the remnants of stars that have reached the end of their life, can have unexpected colors. Unlike most stars which change color based on their temperature, white dwarfs can have shades of green, pink, and purple. The researchers found that this unusual coloration is caused by the interaction of trace elements in the star's atmosphere with the surrounding dense helium plasma. The team used spectra collected by astronomers to calculate how each star's light would appear to human eyes, revealing that some white dwarfs can appear green, yellow, pink, or purple due to the enrichment of their atmospheres with elements from rocky debris. The study suggests that about one in thirty white dwarfs across the Universe could have unusual coloring, with some stars being even more vibrantly colored than others.

cards.title: Honeybee colony can be considered as a single living Organism
cards.content: A new study proposes that a honey bee colony functions as a superorganism, meaning a group of individual bees that work together like the specialized cells of a single living organism. Researchers suggest that the colony has its own life cycle, including development, reproduction through swarming (when a queen leaves with part of the colony to establish a new hive), aging, and eventual death. This perspective challenges conventional beekeeping practices such as frequently replacing queens and preventing swarming, as these interventions may disrupt the colony’s natural reproductive cycle and ability to manage parasites such as Varroa mites. However, further research is needed to determine whether managing colonies according to this superorganism model can improve bee health and parasite control

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: Experimental Treatment Shows Promise for C. Difficile Infections
cards.content: An experimental treatment for C. difficile gut infections, which can cause life-threatening diarrhea, has shown promise in early laboratory and mouse research. The treatment, argyrin B, specifically kills the bacteria responsible for the infection while sparing the rest of the gut microbiome. This is significant because broad-spectrum antibiotics can disrupt the gut's microbial community, allowing C. difficile to multiply unchecked. The researchers believe that argyrin B could reduce the risk of further microbiome disruption, infections, and relapses, which often require a stool transplant. The team plans to continue studying the treatment, including determining the effective dose and testing its ability to prevent recurrent infections.

cards.title: Experimental treatment shows promise against C. difficile
cards.content: Experimental treatment for C. difficile gut infections, which is caused by an imbalance in the gut's microbial community, has shown promise in early laboratory and mouse research. The treatment, argyrin B, specifically kills the C. difficile bacteria while sparing the rest of the gut microbiome. Researchers have found that argyrin B is highly effective against C. difficile infections, reducing the bacterial load in laboratory experiments and mouse models. The compound acts by targeting a specific antibacterial site in the C. difficile bacteria and has shown little to no effect on beneficial microorganisms in the digestive tract. This could lead to a treatment that reduces the risk of further microbiome disruption, infections, and relapses, and may provide an alternative to the current treatment, fecal microbiota transfer, which is complex and unpleasant for many patients.

cards.title: Fat Before Carbs Regulates Blood Sugar in Mice Study
cards.content: In a breakthrough study, researchers found that eating fat before carbohydrates can help regulate blood sugar levels by slowing down stomach emptying and reducing the initial spike. This effect was observed in mice and may be applicable to humans, offering a potential dietary strategy to manage post-meal blood sugar rises, an important treatment target in diabetes.

cards.title: Avalanche Sweeps Away Over 100 Sheep in Himachal Pradesh
cards.content: In October 2025, Joginder Chand, a 50-year-old shepherd from Himachal Pradesh's Chamba district, set out to migrate his 600 sheep and goats to warmer grazing grounds in Kangra district. Suddenly, an avalanche swept away over 100 animals.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

sections.title: Entertainment
sections.description: Stories from film, music, sports, culture and the world of entertainment.

cards.title: Sunderland Music City gets £156,166 grant for heritage project
cards.content: A major heritage project, Sunderland Music City's Mackem Music Memories, has been awarded £156,166 by the National Lottery Heritage Fund to preserve the city's musical history. The project aims to collect over 300 memories of Sunderland's music scene from residents past and present through questionnaires, research, and interviews. The memories will be displayed in an exhibition at the Culture House Sunderland in summer 2027, along with community activities and live events. The project will also work with diverse communities, including South Asian, Filipino, Nigerian, and Eastern European groups, and international students. The goal is to capture these stories before they disappear and make them part of Sunderland's permanent heritage.

cards.title: Paul Shipper: From Film Fan to Illustrator of Marvel and Star Wars
cards.content: Paul Shipper, a film fan-turned-illustrator, has come a long way from creating movie poster artwork for fun. He has worked on some of Hollywood's biggest franchises, including Marvel, Indiana Jones, and Star Wars. Shipper's passion for illustration started when he was a kid, inspired by the films of George Lucas and Steven Spielberg. He shared his designs online, which led to opportunities that once seemed like a dream. The illustrator has worked on various projects, including posters and artwork for blockbuster titles, and has maintained a consistent artistic style despite working across different projects. Shipper is now involved in a charity exhibition, AMPjam Presents: We've Been Framed, which brings together more than 60 artists from around the world to create original artworks inspired by films and television shows.

cards.title: Scottish Actor Hopes Fans Accept His Accent in Marvel Series
cards.content: Scottish actor Ruaridh Mollica, who plays Tommy Maximoff in the Marvel Cinematic Universe miniseries VisionQuest, hopes fans will accept his Scottish accent. He says speaking in his own accent helped him bring the character to life, and he's excited to be part of the show.

cards.title: Criminals use AI to create fake UK retailers, warns National Trading Standards
cards.content: Beware of online scams, warns National Trading Standards, as criminals are using artificial intelligence (AI) to create fake websites and convincing fake products. These scams often claim to be family-owned UK retailers selling quality products, but the reality is that products either don't arrive or are cheap imports from countries like China. AI-generated images, voice cloning, and deepfake videos are all being used to trick people out of their money. Old tactics like spotting typos and grammatical errors are no longer reliable, as AI can now mimic legitimate-looking websites. To protect yourself, stop and think before paying or sharing personal information, and be wary of pressure or urgency. You can report fraud and scams to Report Fraud or by calling the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline.

cards.title: UK Chancellor Plans to Tax Bank Sector
cards.content: UK Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, with the biggest four banks making about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year. The move has been met with resistance from the sector, which warns it will weaken competitiveness and discourage investment and job creation.
